paper_title: CaPtain: A Pipeline for Post-Training Code-as-Policy Robot Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Across coding, web, and tool-use tasks, language-model agents are now routinely trained with the same recipe: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to learn the interface, then multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) to master it. Code-as-policy (CaP) casts robot manipulation in the same form, as the policy writes code against robot APIs and reads back the results, so the same recipe should apply. Yet existing CaP agents sidestep training: they either prompt closed frontier models or delegate manipulation to pre-trained vision-language-action models (VLAs) and high-level skills, while small open vision-language models (VLMs) fail outright. We present CaPtain, an open post-training pipeline that turns a small open VLM into a capable CaP agent, with no VLA, frontier model, or privileged state at test time. CaPtain trains and deploys the policy inside CaPtain-Harness, which exposes low-level perception, geometry, and guarded-motion primitives across simulation and real hardware. We first align the base model via SFT on synthetic trajectories generated with GPT-6 Astra, then apply multi-turn RL. Multi-turn RL must credit tens of agent requests, whose physical effects often surface turns later, from a single end-of-episode outcome. We therefore introduce a physical critic that reads privileged simulator state, never seen by the policy, and credits each request by how much it changes the predicted chance of success. Starting from Qwen3.5-4B (0% zero-shot), CaPtain-4B reaches 55.4% held-out LIBERO success after SFT and 73.8% after RL. On LIBERO-PRO, it reaches 78.5%, surpassing several frontier-model agents, and its RL gains persist across three perturbation suites (+17.6 to +21.2 points). Without target-domain training, it attains 83.3% on SimplerEnv WidowX, exceeds frontier models on CaP-Bench, and runs on a real robot after simulation-only adaptation. We release all code, data, and model weights.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Language-model agents have improved rapidly in coding, web navigation, and tool use, and much of this progress follows common recipe: the agent acts inside fixed execution harness, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) teaches it the interface, and multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) refines its behavior from the outcomes of its own interactions [19, 25, 26, 72]. Code-as-policy (CaP) agents [27, 43, 58] give robot manipulation the same form: the policy observes camera images, writes programs against perception and motion APIs, and reads back what happened. Since the program is composed at test time, CaP agent inherits much of the generalization of the language model that writes it, and frontier models have made this approach strikingly capable. Used directly as robot policy, GPT-6 Astra ranks above every public entry on the RoboDojo leaderboard [90], and with coding harness it solves 94.0% of LIBERO-PRO episodes [67]. This raises natural question: Can small open model be trained into such CaP agent with the same SFT-and-RL recipe, rather than relying on frontier model at test time? In practice, existing CaP agents sidestep training, and in doing so hand the manipulation itself to components the agent cannot learn to improve. One line of work prompts closed frontier models without weight updates [13, 39, 40, 50, 93]. These systems come with high finical cost of calling frontier models in each episode [13, 39, 93], cannot be fine-tuned for new robots or tasks, and cannot run on onboard compute. Another line delegates manipulation to pre-trained vision-language-action models (VLAs) or high-level skills. PyRUA trains 4B coder over frozen VLA and motion planner [67], AgenticRoboRL trains planner around frozen LIBERO-trained VLA [48], SenseNova-RoboRSI builds 27B agent around reusable skills and optional VLA calls [64], and Gemini 4 Argon exposes code-as-policies through skills such as grasp and place [22]. In these systems, the code decides which skill to call, but the skill decides how to grasp, approach, and place. Therefore, the agent stays bounded by the data on which the skill was trained, and RL can at best learn to sequence it. Small open vision-language models (VLMs), meanwhile, fail outright when asked to control robot directly. Qwen3.5-4B solves none of the LIBERO episodes in our harness, and the few efforts that train such models rely mainly on SFT [45] or single-turn text-only RL [20]. What is missing is complete SFT-and-RL recipe that teaches small open VLM to manipulate through low-level primitives, with every manipulation decision made by the policy itself. Applying the recipe at this low level is harder than at the skill level, for reason that does not arise for language agents. Without semantic skills such as grasp and place, the policy must itself decide where to grasp, from which direction to approach, and when to close the gripper, and these decisions are spread over tens of requests per episode, most of which only perceive or verify. Multi-turn RL must then credit these requests, whose physical effects often surface several turns later, with single outcome observed only at the end of the episode. Outcome-only RL assigns the same credit to every request, while language-model critic would have to infer physical progress indirectly from text and images. Robot learning, however, offers an asymmetry that language agents lack: training runs in simulation, where exact object poses, grasp states, and sub-goal progress are known, even though the deployed policy must act from its cameras alone. critic can thus read the physical state that the policy cannot see, and credit each request by how much it moves the task toward success, while the policy itself still acts from its cameras at test time. We present CaPtain, an open post-training pipeline built on these two observations. CaPtain trains and deploys the policy inside CaPtain-Harness, an execution environment that exposes 22 low-level perception, geometric measurement, and guarded-motion primitives and nothing higher. There are no grasp, place, or open-drawer skills and no VLA. Perception returns masks and points, and motion takes an explicit end-effector pose or gripper command. Every call returns structured text receipt reporting what physically happened, such as measured poses, contact forces, or why motion stopped, and the policy-facing API is unchanged across LIBERO [44], RoboTwin 2.0 [11], RoboDojo [10], SimplerEnv [38], CaP-Bench [20], and physical robot. We first apply SFT on in-harness trajectories generated with GPT-6 Astra, rendered in exactly the multi-turn format the policy sees at deployment. We then run multi-turn RL with simulator critic that reads privileged physical state hidden from the policy and credits each request by how much it changes the predicted chance of success, combining the streaming RL formulation of SAO [25] with asymmetric actor-critic training [56]. Since this change is measured at fixed time index, requests that only perceive or verify receive near-zero credit, and credit concentrates on grasps and placements. The critic is used only during training. At test time, the policy relies on camera images and receipts alone. 2 Applying CaPtain to Qwen3.5-4B yields CaPtain-4B, which raises the held-out LIBERO success from 0% to 55.4% after SFT and to 73.8% after RL. On LIBERO-PRO, CaPtain-4B reaches 78.5%, above frontier-model agents such as K1 [40] (77.2%), WAA [93] (75.6%), and ASPIRE [50] (71.7%). RL also gains more when it acts on low-level primitives: across the four LIBERO-PRO suites it adds 19.4 points to our SFT model, whereas RL over frozen VLA adds 5.9 points in AgenticRoboRL [48], although the two start from different baselines. These gains persist under perturbation, ranging from +17.6 to +21.2 points across LIBERO-PRO [97], LIBERO-Plus [18], and LIBERO-MAX [95], with all seven LIBERO-Plus perturbation dimensions improving significantly; by contrast, reported results for end-to-end policies show π0.5 [55] falling from 97% on LIBERO to 12.8% on LIBERO-PRO [97] and the RL-tuned RIPT-VLA [68] scoring no higher than its base model on LIBERO-Plus [18]. Without target-domain training, CaPtain-4B reaches 83.3% on SimplerEnv WidowX, scores 75.0 on CaP-Bench, above frontier models and 7B coder trained with RL on that benchmark, and completes tasks on physical robot after adaptation in coarse simulated twin alone. Transfer remains limited on RoboTwin 2.0 and RoboDojo (22.6% and 0.8% success), which require dual-arm coordination and unfamiliar arm kinematics. Together, these results suggest that robot manipulation over low-level execution harness can be post-trained like any other language agent. Contributions. 1. CaPtain, an open, end-to-end SFT-and-RL pipeline that turns small open VLM into standalone CaP agent. We release the SFT data, the training code and the CaPtain-4B weights. 2. CaPtain-Harness, portable execution harness with low-level primitives only, exposing 22 perception, measurement, and guarded-motion capabilities with grounded text receipts. 3. simulator critic for multi-turn VLM agents that converts privileged physical state transitions into dense per-request credit, with analyses showing that credit concentrates on physical manipulation decisions. 4. comprehensive evaluation showing that RL gains persist across three perturbation suites, that 4B policy surpasses several frontier-model agents at small fraction of their cost, and that it transfers zero-shot across benchmarks and embodiments and to physical robot without real-world data.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Code-as-policy robot agents. Code as Policies [43] and VoxPoser [27] showed that language model can control robot by writing programs over perception and control APIs. Recent agents scale this idea with frontier models and richer harnesses. GPT-6 Astra, used directly as robot policy, ranks above every public entry on RoboDojo [90], and Gemini 4 Argon exposes code-as-policies as developer workflow built around skills such as grasp and place [22]. Many systems reach their headline results with frontier models and no weight updates, including ASPIRE [50], RATs [88], RHO [16], RACaP [39], OpenRUA [13], RoboDawn [24], Encore [28] and RoboRSI [77]; OpenRUA, for example, reaches 91.8 on LIBERO-PRO at $822 per episode. Others orchestrate frozen VLA as skill, including Harness VLA [94], PyRUA [67], Pigey [21] and AgenticRoboRL [48, 81], or give the agent privileged simulator state or success oracle at test time [40, 69, 93]. Training the code-writing model itself has received less attention. CaP-X [20] applies GRPO to single-turn, text-only 7B coder on three Robosuite tasks. Guava [45] trains Qwen3.5-4B mainly by SFT and adds GRPO on two MuJoCo tasks. PyRUA trains 4B coder with GRPO on top of VLA and motion-planning primitives [67], SenseNova-RoboRSI releases 27B agent that improves itself through reusable skills [64], and AgenticRoboRL trains 9B planner by SFT and multi-turn RL around VLA trained on LIBERO [48]. CaPtain instead post-trains small open VLM end-to-end directly over low-level perception and motion primitives, operating at test time from camera observations and execution receipts alone. End-to-end robot policies. Vision-language-action models (VLAs) such as OpenVLA [30], OpenVLA-OFT [31], π0 [2], π0.5 [55], GR00T [52, 53] and RDT [47] learn from large demonstration corpora and reach 9498% on standard LIBERO. World-action models (WAMs) build on video-generation pretraining and predict future observations together with actions, e.g. OpenWAM-α [76], the composable OpenWAM framework of Yu et al. [83], and others [73, 79]. growing line of work post-trains VLAs with RL [9, 36, 46, 49, 68, 85], which raises in-distribution success. Perturbation suites such as LIBERO-PRO, LIBERO-Plus and LIBEROMAX [18, 95, 97] test whether these abilities generalize, and they show that end-to-end policies remain 3 Figure 2 Overview of CaPtain. Top: inference, one episode in CaPtain-Harness: at each request the policy writes Python cell against low-level API and receives text receipts and new images, for up to 60 requests. Bottom: training and test: SFT on synthetic agent trajectories, then RL in which simulator critic turns privileged physical state into per-request credit; the critic is removed at test time. sensitive to changes in objects, layouts and instructions. For example, π0.5 drops from 97% on standard LIBERO to 12.8% under the LIBERO-PRO position and task perturbations [97], and on LIBERO-Plus, RL post-training with RIPT-VLA scores 68.4 against 69.6 for its base OpenVLA-OFT [18, 68]. We study the same question for policy that writes code, and find that its RL gains persist across all three suites (4.1). Credit assignment and privileged critics. PPO [63] with GAE [62] and critic-free GRPO [65] are the standard tools for LLM RL. For long multi-turn episodes, turn-level credit [3, 8, 19, 37, 42, 71, 74, 78, 87, 91, 98] and value estimation [29] are active topics, and SAO [25] shows that streaming RL with co-trained language-model critic scales to frontier LLM agents. The works closest to our credit mechanism turn state-value or progress difference into turn-level credit, using an exact game solver (CAST [75]), hand-written acceptance checks (ProCredit [51]), frozen distance estimator (T2SPO [86]) or rule-based predicates over simulator state (DLS [12]). Privileged critics for LLMs appear in SWEET-RL [99], Le Critique [70], KAT-Coder [26] and Odysseus [66], but none of them reads physical state. In robotics, asymmetric actor-critic [56] gives the critic full simulator state while the actor sees images, with analyses of its bias under partial observability [1, 15], privileged teachers are distilled into sensorimotor students [7, 33, 35], and privileged critics have been used with non-language actors on LIBERO [89, 92]. CaPtain carries the asymmetric template to language-model actor that writes code: since continuous manipulation offers neither solver nor checklist, it learns value over privileged physics and turns its changes into per-request credit.

sections.title: 3 CaPtain
sections.content: CaPtain converts small open vision-language model into code-as-policy agent by coupling fixed, portable execution harness (3.1) with in-harness supervised fine-tuning on synthetic trajectories (3.2) and multi-turn reinforcement learning guided by simulator critic (3.3), as illustrated in Figure 2. The harness defines the low-level action space and receipt feedback loop, SFT aligns the model to this interaction protocol, and RL optimizes closed-loop manipulation and recovery within the same environment. Hyperparameters and infrastructure details are provided in Appendix A.

Each request is single model call. The policy first reasons in its thinking channel and then emits one or more calls to the python tool, so at πθ( ht) contains both the reasoning and the code. The harness executes the calls in order, appends their outputs (cell results, receipts and images) as ot+1, and issues the next request with the updated history. The loop ends when reply contains no tool call, normally right after finish(), or when budget on requests, physical actions or wall time is exhausted. The overall design of CaPtain-Harness is summarized in Figure 7 (Appendix A). Context management. long episode does not fit in the context window of small model, so the harness manages the history explicitly. Tool outputs are truncated to fixed token budget, at most 20 receipt lines are printed per cell, and only the 12 most recent images are kept. When the history approaches the context limit, the harness compacts it turn by turn. It keeps the initial task context and the most recent turns verbatim, and replaces the removed turns with short notice that lists the commands they ran and warns that the scene may have changed since. Because the agents variables live in the Python session rather than in the prompt, detections, poses and helper functions survive compaction. Compaction behaves identically during RL rollouts and at test time, so the policy is trained on the inputs it will see. persistent Python session. The only tool is python, sandboxed Python session with pre-imported robot module. Variables persist across requests, so the agent can store detections, poses and its own helper functions and reuse them later. Robot calls do not raise exceptions; each returns structured result with success flag, failure category, message and value. This lets the agent write ordinary control flow (if, loops, retries) around robot calls within single request. Low-level primitives only. The robot module exposes 22 capabilities plus finish() (Appendix B): perception: observe (head and wrist RGB-D), segment (text-prompted masks from SAM 3 [6]), point (pointing with Molmo2 [14]), mark_point (back-projects pixel the model chose itself) and track_target; measurement: measure_object_geometry (center, extents, yaw and the offset to destination), contact and release geometry checks, and comparisons of an object across observations; motion: move_to (an absolute end-effector pose, or single jaw command), hold, recover (a bounded reversal along the last trajectory) and release; planning and state: read-only reachability and timing checks, robot state and pose arithmetic. There are no grasp, place or open-drawer skills and no VLA. The agent must decide where to grasp, from which direction to approach and when to close the jaw. The harness turns each move_to into straight Cartesian motion, solves inverse kinematics, checks self-collision and monitors force at every control substep, stopping at first contact unless the agent requests manipulation mode that tolerates load. Because every approach vector, grasp pose, and jaw command is written explicitly in Python, the full manipulation policy is exposed to language-model post-training. Receipts. After each robot call, the harness appends short receipt to the cell output that reports what physically happened: for motions, the stop reason, the executed distance, the peak force and the jaw opening before and after; for perception, the detection identity, its metric position and its offset to the destination. The agent can also attach up to four camera images per cell. Receipts give the policy dense, grounded feedback in text that complements the images. 5 Self-verification and success. completion gate on the host checks the agents own recorded measurements and may reject finish() twice before accepting it. Host success is the benchmarks goal predicate, evaluated by the environment host on the final state. Strict success additionally requires that the agent ended the episode with finish(), since robot that does not declare completion cannot be deployed. Portability. The policy-facing API is unchanged across LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, RoboDojo, SimplerEnv, CaP-Bench and the real robot; backend adapters, some of which add benchmark-specific safeguards, are listed in Appendix L.

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: Benchmarks. We train only on the 40 original LIBERO tasks [44] and evaluate on LIBERO and three perturbation suites built on them, whose perturbations never appear in training. LIBERO uses the official held-out initial states 1116 of all 40 tasks (240 episodes). LIBERO-PRO [97] perturbs object positions and task semantics across the four suites (100 episodes per subset); following prior work, we report the short-horizon 3-suite average (Spatial, Object, Goal; 600 episodes) and the full 4-suite average (adding Long; 800 episodes), as well as its 4-category split (160 episodes). LIBERO-Plus [18] is evaluated on stratified sample of 700 cases across its seven perturbation dimensions. LIBERO-MAX [95] uses its 80 Lite cases under Base (static) and Dynamic (in-episode) perturbations. For zero-shot transfer we use RoboTwin 2.0 [11], RoboDojo [10], SimplerEnv [38] and CaP-Bench [20] (4.3). Protocol and metrics. All evaluations run in CaPtain-Harness with the settings of RL rollouts: temperature 1, thinking enabled, at most 60 requests, 150 physical actions and 1,080 per episode, and no early stopping. At test time, the simulator critic is removed and all object coordinates are estimated online from RGB-D camera observations and execution receipts. We report host success, the benchmark predicate on the final state, and strict success, which additionally requires that the agent ended the episode with finish(). Comparisons between our models are paired on identical (suite, task, initial-state) triples, with exact two-sided McNemar tests and 95% task-cluster bootstrap intervals. Models and baselines. CaPtain-4B-SFT is the model after Stage 1, which also initializes RL and serves as the KL reference. We use the checkpoint at round 300 (75 optimizer updates) as CaPtain-4B. Baseline numbers are taken from the respective papers.

sections.title: 4.4 Transfer to a real robot
sections.content: We also test whether the pipeline carries over to real robot through CaPtain-Harness. The simulator is replaced by hardware backend for an Astrabot XR1 arm with head RGB-D camera, wrist camera, kinematic twin updated from the measured joints, and safety guards. The policy-facing API and receipts are unchanged, and the critic is not used. Because the XR1 arm differs from the simulated Panda in kinematics, reach, gripper geometry and camera placement, we use checkpoint fine-tuned on episodes from coarse twin simulation of the XR1, which teaches the policy the conventions of the new embodiment. The twin uses primitive objects and untextured surfaces and does not reconstruct the real scene (Figure 6); the policy is adapted with simulated XR1 episodes only and uses no real-world data. Figure 6 The twin simulation used to adapt the policy to the XR1 arm (left) and the real scene at test time (right). Figure 5 shows two tasks with new objects and layouts. In the first, the agent puts yellow cube into wooden tray. In the second, the instruction refers to the objects only indirectly, so the agent must first resolve which 12 cube has the color of the sky and which container is not round before it can act. Both tasks are completed with the same low-level primitives used in simulation. Appendix gives step-by-step traces of both episodes.

sections.title: 4.5 Analysis of the simulator critic
sections.content: To understand what the simulator critic learns and why it stabilizes multi-turn RL, we analyze offline rollouts from an earlier 9B policy (15k episodes, 573k request states) alongside training-time logs. Value ranking and credit concentration. The critic predicts final episode success with an overall AUC of 0.970, within-group AUC of 0.904 across rollouts sharing the same start state, and calibration error of 0.006 (the warm-start critic used for 4B RL achieves 0.907 held-out AUC). Because the one-step TD difference (Eq. 5) holds the request index fixed, credit concentrates sharply on turns that alter the physical scene: successful grasps receive median of +0.058 (IQR [0.036, 0.090]) and failed grasps receive 0.0075, whereas perception-only requests receive 0.0002. Aggregated over whole trajectories, 65% of the total mass is assigned to motions, 14% to grasps, and 14% to releases, while perception-only turns account for just 1.3%. Why policy-side features and LM hidden states are excluded. When counters of the policys own actions (e.g., cumulative perception or failed calls) are provided to the critic, within-group AUC on pre-grasp states rises from 0.773 to 0.862, but these counters act as proxies for elapsed time and leak negative credit onto perception turns. Similarly, linear probe on the language models hidden state decodes the request index with R2=0.80; feeding hidden states to the critic shifts 35% of the total mass onto perception requests. Restricting the critic inputs to privileged physical state and evaluating at fixed time index prevents this credit leakage and reduces the gradient-noise scale on 9B SFT rollouts from 9.0k episodes under outcome-only GRPO to 6.7k episodes (λ=0.9; Appendix H).

sections.title: 5 Limitations
sections.content: Single-benchmark RL training and bimanual control. Our RL stage is trained exclusively on the 40 LIBERO tasks with single 7-DoF arm. While CaPtain-4B transfers zero-shot to unseen single-arm tasks and embodiments, cross-benchmark performance remains below in-domain accuracy, and tasks requiring simultaneous bimanual coordination or tight kinematic reach on unfamiliar 6-DoF arms are not yet addressed (4.3). Privileged state during RL. Training the simulator critic relies on exact simulator state. In our offline sensitivity study, replacing ground-truth object poses with noisy estimates degrades correlation with the privileged (0.49 under 2 cm pose noise, 0.36 under 5 cm, and 0.21 using the policys own perception), indicating that online RL directly on physical hardware would require an external state estimator. Interface and SFT coverage. The agents action space is bounded by the 22 capabilities of CaPtain-Harness and the behaviors demonstrated in the synthetic SFT trajectories (Appendix C). Tasks that require continuous force-controlled compliancesuch as Wipe on CaP-Bench, which demands sustained downward pressingcannot be expressed by guarded Cartesian position primitives.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented CaPtain, an open post-training pipeline that turns 4B vision-language model into standalone code-as-policy robot agent operating directly over low-level perception and motion primitives. By pairing portable execution harness (CaPtain-Harness) with synthetic SFT trajectories and multi-turn RL guided by privileged simulator critic, CaPtain converts sparse episode outcomes into dense per-request credit concentrated on physical manipulation decisions, while requiring no privileged information, demonstrationtrained VLA skills, or frontier API calls at test time. Across held-out LIBERO and three perturbation suites, CaPtain-4B improves substantially over SFT, matches or surpasses several frontier-model agents at small fraction of their inference cost, transfers zero-shot to unseen benchmarks and embodiments, and deploys on physical robot through simulated embodiment adaptation alone. Extending the simulator critic to value 13 termination decisions, bimanual coordination, and multi-embodiment workspaces offers direct path toward closing the remaining gap to frontier systems.

sections.title: A Implementation details
sections.content: A.1 Policy and harness Figure 7 Design of CaPtain-Harness. The policy writes Python into persistent session ① that exposes only low-level primitives ②; motions are executed with IK and guarded contact ③, every call returns receipt ④, completion gate checks the agents own measurements ⑤, and environment-specific backends sit below the API ⑥. Receipt values are illustrative. Policy. The policy πθ is Qwen3.5-4B [59]: 32 layers with hybrid Gated-DeltaNet and full attention, plus 24-layer vision tower. It is served with vLLM [34] and sampled at temperature 1 with top-p 1, in training and in evaluation. Each request is one chat completion of at most 4,096 tokens with thinking enabled. The request uses the same chat template (system prompt, developer messages with TASK.md, tool schema) as the SFT trajectories, so training data and policy requests have identical format. The completion may contain calls to single tool, python. The context window is 65,536 tokens, and older turns are compacted beyond 60k tokens. The python tool and receipts. The python tool executes code inside persistent, sandboxed Python 3.11 session (numpy, scipy, Pillow) with pre-imported robot client module, allowing variables and helper functions to persist across requests. Robot calls never raise exceptions; instead, each returns structured dictionary {success, executed, failure_category, message, value, diagnostics, budget} alongside concise (300-character) text receipt appended to the cell output. Motion receipts report the stop reason, executed distance, peak contact force, and jaw opening before and after execution, whereas perception receipts report the detection identifier, metric position, and object-to-destination offset. The policy may attach up to four camera images per cell, with the conversation history retaining the twelve most recent images. Robot API. The API has 22 capabilities plus finish() (full list in Appendix B). They fall into five groups: Perception: observe (head and wrist RGB-D at 512512), segment (SAM 3 [6]), point (Molmo2-8B [14]), mark_point (back-projects pixel the model chose itself), select_detection and track_target. Measurement: measure_object_geometry, measure_image_points, inspect_contact_geometry, inspect_release_geometry and compare_object_observations. Motion: move_to, hold, recover and release. move_to takes either an absolute end-effector pose or single jaw command. Planning: the read-only checks check_motion and preview_motion. State: get_robot_state, gripper_state, robot_geometry, read_motion_trajectory and transform_pose. 20 There are no grasp or place macros. The policy must choose poses, approach directions and jaw commands itself. Motions are straight Cartesian sweeps executed by an operational-space controller. Damped leastsquares IK and self-collision checks run before execution, and per-substep force monitoring applies guarded stop at first contact or tolerates load in manipulation mode. TASK.md tells the policy the instruction, the API, the coordinate frames and the standards by which the final scene is judged. host-side completion gate checks only the agents own recorded measurements, never simulator state. It can reject finish() twice; third call is accepted. Budgets and success. An episode may use at most 60 requests, 1,080 of wall time and 150 physical actions (120 during RL). Host success is the benchmarks goal predicate evaluated on the final state. Strict success additionally requires that the agent ended the episode by calling finish(). false finish is finish() on failed state. Strict success is the deployable metric: robot that never declares completion cannot be used. A.2 RL Privileged state. Before each request t, the environment server records hidden snapshot that the policy cannot access. From this mark we compute 36 features x(st): end-effector position and jaw state; goal bookkeeping: number of goals, number and fraction satisfied, active goal, and whether that goal involves joint (articulated part) or contact; distances: target to goal (raw and normalized), end-effector to target, and target to destination; target lift and displacement, maximum displacement of any object, and the nearest-other-object distance; joint position and change for articulated goals, plus held and ever-held flags. Counters of the policys own behavior, such as the number of perception calls or failed calls, are excluded so that elapsed time does not leak into the value estimate (4.5). 5 (cid:80)5 Critic. The critic Vϕ(s, t) = σ(cid:0) 1 k=1 fϕk ([x(s); t; onehot(task)])(cid:1) is an ensemble of five MLPs (three hidden layers of 256 units) whose logits are averaged. It predicts the probability of host success from the current state. We include the request index explicitly but hold it fixed inside each difference (below), so elapsed time does not leak into the credit. The critic is warm-started on 1,000 episodes of an earlier policy (45k request states, held-out AUC 0.907, Brier 0.075). It is then co-trained online as in SAO: after each round of 256 episodes it takes two AdamW steps of binary cross-entropy against host success over all request states of that round. Each rounds advantages use the critic before that rounds update. Advantage. For episode with requests = 1, . . . , , we define: δt = ct + Vϕ(st+1, t) Vϕ(st, t) (t < ), δT = cT + Ri Vϕ(sT , ), (9) and AGAE group-relative outcome term: = (cid:80) k λkδt+k with λ = 0.9 and no discount [62]. Each start state is rolled out G=4 times. We add Ai,t = (cid:0)Gi Ggroup (cid:1) + (cid:0)AGAE i,t AGAE i, (cid:1), Gi = Ri + (cid:80) ct, (10) and divide by running estimate of the advantage standard deviation, without re-centering. All tokens of request share the advantage Ai,t. Holding fixed inside each difference prevents elapsed time from leaking into δt, while online co-training keeps the value estimate calibrated to the improving policy. Physical state changes only through physical actions, so the one-step term Vϕ(st+1, t) Vϕ(st, t) is near zero for requests that only perceive, regardless of how many tokens they contain. Such requests still receive credit through GAE from the physical actions they enable, and through the group outcome term. Returns and costs. The terminal return Ri is: 1 for host success with finish(); 0.25 for success without finish() (a missed finish); 0.3 for false finish; 0.1 when budget is exhausted; 0 for any other failure. The immediate costs ct 0 penalize: physical actions beyond 1.5 the median action count of the tasks SFT episodes (0.008 each); failed or rejected physical actions (0.02 each); actions and requests after the host first judges the scene solved (capped at 0.45 in total). The post-success cost pushes the policy to declare completion; without it, the missed-finish rate rose to about 20% (Appendix E). For the eight hardest tasks (four from libero_10 and four from libero_goal) we add staged one-shot subgoal reward. failed episode that reaches rung of an n-rung ladder (grasp, lift, place, joint opened, . . . ) receives 0.15 d/(n+1) 0.1125. Rungs are judged from hidden snapshots; place rungs and rungs for moving an object toward its goal must still hold at the end. The resulting ordering is: success > missed finish > partial progress > 0 > budget exhaustion > false finish. Policy update. Following SAO [25], we use single-pass, streaming RL with double-sided token masking (unlike SAO, with groups of G=4 rollouts per start). token is kept only if 0.2 < πθ/πrollout < 4.0; it is then weighted by that ratio. We also apply k3 KL penalty to the SFT model (β=0.002) on kept tokens. At most 8 requests per trajectory are trained, sampled uniformly and inclusion-weighted; the critic still uses all requests. Gradients are accumulated over K=4 rounds of 256 episodes (64 start groups 4), i.e. 1,024 episodes per optimizer step, matching the empirical gradient-noise scale (Appendix H). We use AdamW with constant learning rate of 4.24 106 after warm-up, full fine-tuning with FSDP2, and at most two policy versions of staleness. Training distribution. RL samples from pool of 7,360 fresh start states over all 40 LIBERO tasks (spatial, object, goal, long), of which 649 libero_object starts with degenerate goal region are never drawn: 5,600 wide-layout starts with light, camera and material perturbations; 1,760 official initial states. The 240 official states used for evaluation (indices 1116 of each task) are never drawn. To save rollout time, the critic also stops rollouts early: an episode is ended when Vϕ < 0.02 for five consecutive requests, except in 5% control slice and on the hard tasks. cut episode settles as budget-exhausted (R=0.1), so the critic also shapes returns. held-out monitor stream (every tenth episode) receives no gradient. Infrastructure and compute. The trainer occupies 8 H100s. second 8-GPU node serves 6 vLLM policy servers, SAM 3 and Molmo, and renders 6480 concurrent MuJoCo episodes. Weights are synchronized to vLLM by NCCL in under 1 s. round takes 8121,053 on 16 GPUs. Per request, generation takes about 2.6 of the 6.7 wall time, and the environment, tools and perception take the rest. The main checkpoint, CaPtain-4B, has seen 300 rounds, i.e. 75 optimizer updates on 76,800 episodes, at about 1,290 H100-hours (derived from wall time). The last 8 rounds ran on single 8-GPU node (trainer world size 4, resharded; 1,5511,626 per round) with the RL hyperparameters unchanged.

Equivalence of each rewrite was checked call site by call site against mock robot, and replaying 6 rewritten episodes changed robot commands by less than 1 cm. Turns with repeated execution failures or recovery loops (about 3.6% of requests) are masked from the loss, as are requests after gate-rejected finish on one long-horizon task. Training. Only assistant turns are supervised. text-hint mask replaces earlier mark_point pixel coordinates in the history with <masked> with probability 0.2. This forces the model to look at the image instead of copying coordinates. Training uses full fine-tuning of the language model with the vision tower frozen. The batch is 16 packed rows of at most 66k tokens. We use DeepSpeed ZeRO-3 in bf16, gradient clipping at 1.0, and 2,435 steps (1.5 epochs). The final model scores 42/80 on our 80-episode validation set. Diversity of tasks and layouts during post-training Diversity of tasks and scene layouts in the post-training data is essential for keeping the visual grounding of the base model. In an earlier version of our data, most episodes started from the official LIBERO initial states, in which each object occupies nearly the same position across episodes (per-object position standard deviation about 1.4 cm). Models fine-tuned on these data learned to reproduce object positions from the task identity 23 rather than reading them from the image: replacing the input image left the likelihood of the predicted pixel coordinates unchanged. The policy had effectively memorized the layouts and lost the vision-language models ability to ground objects in new scenes. We therefore collect SFT data on wide-layout starts, whose per-object position standard deviation is about 15 cm, mix all task suites, and randomize lighting, camera pose and materials during RL. With this diversity, the model grounds every mark_point and segment call in the current image, which is also what allows it to transfer to the unseen objects and layouts of the real-robot tasks (4.4). Reward, costs and early stopping The post-success cost (every physical action at 0.008 plus 0.005 per request after the host first judges success, capped at 0.45) was introduced after an earlier run in which missed finishes rose to about 20% per round. The action costs were introduced after RL inflated the number of move_to calls per request: from 0.69 to 1.05 in successful episodes and from 0.78 to 1.39 in failed ones. The request cap did not constrain the number of actions packed into one request. The staged subgoal reward is one-shot, monotone ladder judged from hidden snapshots. It applies to 8 hard tasks (libero_10 3/6/8/9; goal 0/3/5/7), from round 9 onward. grasp rung requires the object lifted by at least 5 cm with the end-effector within 13 cm. joint rung requires the articulated part to cover at least 20% of its initial distance to the goal position. The critic also stops rollouts early, for speed. An episode is cut when < 0.02 for 5 consecutive requests after request 5. deterministic 5% control slice is never cut. An episode is stopped and settled as missed finish once all goals have held for 15 consecutive requests without finish().

sections.content: Host and strict success diverge late in training (Figure 8). After about round 340, host success holds at about 65% while strict success falls from about 60% to 44%. The lost episodes run out of requests while re-verifying solved scenes, while false finishes stay rare. Because strict success drops between rounds 300 and 400, we use the round-300 checkpoint as CaPtain-4B. The mechanism is over-verification. After the task is solved, the policy keeps measuring, re-observing and comparing instead of calling finish(). The return structure makes this slow drift rather than cliff: missed finish still earns 0.25; the post-success cost is capped; the critic, trained on host success, assigns 1 to every post-success state. The critic therefore gives the decision to stop no credit; only the terminal return and the small post-success request cost distinguish it. We observed the same failure in an earlier run, where it doubled missed finishes 25 Figure 8 Finish collapse. Evaluation of saved checkpoints during RL: 40 official seed-11 episodes plus 40 wide-layout episodes per checkpoint; dots are raw values and lines 5-checkpoint moving average.
